pages.subtitle: The late seventies are shifting faster than our labels.
text_blocks: The mood of 1978 is unmistakable: bright records, crowded cinemas, and television that remains stitched into nightly routine.
We are watching established forms evolve in public. Disco widens, rock adapts, and pop grows more polished without becoming predictable.
This issue tracks those shifts with pages designed to feel like a printed magazine, not a website article stream.
sidebar_items: Music is setting pace for the whole week
Film is scaling up event energy
Television remains the intimate medium
pages.pull_quote: "1978 feels less like an ending than a loud midpoint."

pages.subtitle: How dance-floor records became national fixtures.
text_blocks: By 1978, disco has moved from selective club circuits into mainstream radio and retail shelves.
The production style is deliberate: tight drums, elastic bass, lush strings, and vocal hooks that land immediately.
Listeners now hear dance records in cars, shops, and neighborhood parties, not only under mirrored ceilings.
Whatever its critics say, disco has become a shared social soundtrack.
pages.pull_quote: "A strong dance record can turn strangers into a temporary community."
sidebar_items: Bee Gees remain central to crossover momentum
Donna Summer signals dance-floor urgency
Chic proves groove can be both stylish and precise

pages.subtitle: Taste politics and chart reality in the same week.
text_blocks: Every dominant style attracts a backlash, and disco now sits at the center of that argument.
Some critics dismiss the polish. Fans answer that arrangement craft is exactly why these records hold up.
Meanwhile, chart data keeps validating demand: Bee Gees, Donna Summer, and Chic continue drawing massive audiences.
The disagreement itself proves disco matters culturally, not just commercially.
pages.pull_quote: "People debate disco all week and dance to it anyway."

pages.subtitle: Grease, Superman, and event-film momentum.
text_blocks: 1978 theaters are balancing broad comedy, musicals, suspense, and large-scale hero stories.
Grease and Animal House proved appetite for high-energy crowd experiences.
Superman and The Deer Hunter show opposite ends of scale but equal commitment to cinematic event value.
Box-office queues remain a public ritual that television cannot duplicate.
pages.pull_quote: "A full theater still turns release night into a civic event."

pages.subtitle: Why prime-time structure still shapes household rhythm.
text_blocks: Television remains the most intimate format because it returns on schedule and enters homes without ceremony.
New comedies and workplace formats in 1978 carry faster writing and stronger character contrast.
Programs like Mork and Mindy, WKRP in Cincinnati, and Taxi reflect a changing appetite for tonal mix.
Cinema may own spectacle, but television owns repetition and familiarity.
pages.pull_quote: "A weekly show can become part of household architecture."
